title: Types of lentils and how they differ

seo.title: Types of lentils: brown, green, Puy, beluga and red
seo.meta_description: Whole brown, green and black lentils hold shape better; split red and yellow lentils cook quickly and break down. Compare texture, time and best uses.
seo.search_intent: Distinguish lentil types by seed coat, texture, cooking time and culinary use.

excerpt: The biggest difference is not just color but whether the lentil is whole with its seed coat intact or split and hulled. Brown and green lentils work well in soups and stews; Puy and beluga stay firmer; split red and yellow lentils can cook in about 10–15 minutes and turn creamy.
content_html:
“Lentil” covers several very different cooking behaviors. The most important structural difference is whether the seed is whole with its coat intact or split and hulled. Color helps identify types, but it does not tell the whole texture story.

Brown lentils

Brown lentils are versatile and hold their shape reasonably well if they are not overcooked. They work in soups, stews, taco fillings and grain bowls. Whole lentils generally take around 20–30 minutes, though age and variety shift the exact time.

Green lentils

Green lentils are often a little larger and firmer. They are useful in salads and dishes where distinct lentils matter. Extended cooking eventually makes them split too.

French or Puy-style lentils

These are small, mottled green lentils known for a firmer texture and slightly peppery flavor. True Le Puy lentils come from the protected French growing area; similar lentils grown elsewhere are often labeled French green or Puy-style.

Their firm bite makes them especially useful in salads and side dishes.

Black beluga lentils

Small, glossy and black, beluga lentils resemble caviar and retain their shape well. They suit salads, bowls and plated side dishes. Their cooking time is generally in the same range as other whole lentils, roughly 20–30 minutes.

Red, yellow and orange lentils

These are commonly sold split and hulled. That structure lets them cook much faster, often in 10–15 minutes, and they readily collapse into a creamy texture.

They are ideal for dal, purees and thick soups but a poor choice when you want intact lentils in a salad.

Do they differ much nutritionally?

All lentils provide plant protein, carbohydrate, fiber, iron and folate, but removing the seed coat can reduce some fiber. Variety and cooked water content also change the numbers, so one composition figure should not be applied blindly to every lentil product.

How to choose

TypeTextureTypical use
BrownTender, holds shapeSoups, stews
GreenFirmStews, salads
French/PuyVery firmSalads, sides
Black belugaFirm, smallSalads, bowls
Split red/yellowCreamy, breaks downDal, purees, soups

The practical takeaway

Choose lentils for the final texture you need. For intact lentils, use whole brown, green, French/Puy or beluga types. For fast thickening and a creamy result, choose split red or yellow lentils.

faq.question: Which lentils are best for stew?
faq.answer: Brown and green lentils work well because they become tender while holding shape better than split red lentils.

faq.question: Which lentils are best for salad?
faq.answer: French/Puy and black beluga lentils are especially firm; whole green lentils also work well.

faq.question: Why do red lentils cook faster?
faq.answer: They are commonly split and hulled, so water and heat reach the interior more quickly.
